title: When the Clock Wakes
premise: In 1918 Philadelphia, August Sandoval, a Black woman passing as a man to work as a driver for suffragist Adeline Marsh, reads every letter she delivers and believes history belongs to other people. When a German-American child is left at her door with a note instructing her to forget the face, August recognizes the boy as the son of Ernst Keller, a pacifist correspondent whose letters she has secretly kept—and who has just been declared an enemy alien. To honor a promise made in peacetime, August must hide the child inside the movement's own house while the armistice negotiations stall, risking exposure of both her identity and Adeline's cause. The novel ends with the armistice signed but justice unfinished: August chooses to stop being invisible, testifying on the Kellers' behalf and claiming her own name in print.
about_author: Cyrus Halloran is the pen name of a former archivist who spent a decade cataloging wartime correspondence in Mid-Atlantic historical societies. They write fiction about the people history files under 'miscellaneous.'

chapters.title: The Second Envelope
chapters.summary: August's POV. Establishes her double life: driving Adeline Marsh through suffrage rallies by day, reading intercepted letters by lamplight by night. She opens a letter from Ernst Keller, a German-born pacifist writing to Adeline about a shared prewar promise. Emotional beat: quiet longing for a life where reading other people's futures counts as having one.

chapters.title: Instructions to Forget
chapters.summary: August's POV. A rain-soaked night delivery ends with a child abandoned at the boarding house door, a note pinned to his coat: forget this face. August recognizes Ernst's handwriting. She hides the boy, Tomas, in her room as neighbors knock. Emotional beat: terror sharpening into resolve—the first crack in her belief that invisibility protects anyone.

chapters.title: What the Landlady Knows
chapters.summary: August's POV with a shift into landlady Bess Okafor's perspective mid-chapter. Bess has guessed August is a woman for months and says nothing; now she helps forge papers calling Tomas a nephew. Their bargain deepens into uneasy sisterhood. Emotional beat: belonging offered on dangerous terms—kindness that could burn them both.

chapters.title: Enemy Alien
chapters.summary: Adeline's POV. Federal agents visit the Marsh house hunting registered enemy aliens; Ernst's name appears on a list. Adeline must decide whether the movement can afford scandal or owes him its protection. She notices August flinching at every question. Emotional beat: the cost of principle when principle becomes liability.

chapters.title: Letters Never Sent
chapters.summary: August's POV, interwoven with flashbacks to 1913: how she met Ernst delivering letters between Adeline and his peace circle, and the promise made—that if anything happened, his family would not vanish alone. Present-day August writes to Ernst's interned wife using a dead man's return address. Emotional beat: grief braided with guilt over promises kept only in secret.

chapters.title: The Raid on Vine Street
chapters.summary: Tomas's POV, limited and childlike. Agents raid the German-American neighborhood; Tomas witnesses his aunt detained and barely escapes back to August. His arrival nearly exposes the household. Emotional beat: a child's understanding that forgetting a face is another word for erasing a person.

chapters.title: A House Divided Against Itself
chapters.summary: Adeline's POV. A rival suffrage faction threatens to expose 'the alien child' unless Adeline drops a controversial speech. August confesses everything—Tomas, the letters, and that she is a woman. Adeline's fury gives way to recognition: they have both been passing. Emotional beat: betrayal transmuted into alliance.

chapters.title: Armistice, Almost
chapters.summary: August's POV. Rumors of imminent peace spark street celebrations while the government accelerates deportations; Ernst is transferred to a camp awaiting removal. August realizes the armistice will save no one she loves unless someone speaks. She drafts testimony naming names, including her own. Emotional beat: the pivot from survival to sacrifice.

chapters.title: The Hearing
chapters.summary: Climax, alternating August's and Adeline's POV. At Ernst's deportation hearing, August testifies—removing her cap, speaking as a woman, presenting the preserved letters as evidence of his loyalty and their shared promise. Agents move to detain her; Adeline and Bess rally press and suffragists outside. Emotional beat: visibility chosen at last, at full price.

chapters.title: When the Clock Wakes
chapters.summary: Resolution, August's POV. Armistice bells ring; Ernst is released pending review, Tomas reunited with his father, and August keeps the boy until then. Her testimony appears in the Tribune under her real name. Standing in the crowd she once drove past, she no longer reads history—she is in it. Emotional beat: inheritance claimed; belonging earned, not granted.
